title: Dundee Cake
subtitle: Scottish fruit cake with whole almonds on top
excerpt: Dundee cake is a light fruit cake flavoured with orange zest and whisky, topped with rings of whole blanched almonds. It is less dense than a Christmas cake and needs no marzipan or icing. Serves 12 slices.
sourceNotes: Dundee cake is associated with the Scottish city of Dundee and with the Keiller marmalade company, which is credited with popularising the cake commercially in the late 19th century using surplus orange peel from its marmalade production. Mrs Beeton (1861, Project Gutenberg #10136) does not give a Dundee cake recipe by name, but the format (a light, boiled-fruit-free recipe with almonds on top) is distinct from the darker Christmas cake tradition. F. Marian McNeill, The Scots Kitchen (1929), lists Dundee cake as one of the definitive Scottish bakes. The whole almond topping is its signature; it must not be roughly chopped or flaked.

recipe.freezeNotes: Wrap the cooled cake well and freeze for up to three months. Thaw at room temperature overnight.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Dundee cake improves after two to three days. Wrap in baking parchment and keep in a tin.

glossaryTerms.definition: Whole almonds with their brown skin removed by briefly soaking in boiling water. The pale, white-skinned almonds arranged in concentric rings on top of Dundee cake are one of its defining visual features.

content.text: Dundee cake is a fruit cake made by the creaming method rather than the boil-and-soak method used for Christmas cakes. That difference matters: it is lighter in texture and less sweet, and has a fine crumb rather than a dense, sticky interior. The flavour comes from orange zest, mixed fruit, and a splash of whisky or brandy added to the batter.
The top is the identifying mark: whole

arranged in concentric rings, pressed into the surface before baking. They toast to a golden brown in the oven and remain whole. Do not use flaked or chopped almonds; the whole almond arrangement is not decorative choice but part of what makes it a Dundee cake.

items.prepNote: finely grated zest of 1 large orange

content.text: Prepare the tin and make the batter
Heat the oven to 150°C fan (170°C conventional). Grease and double-line a 20 cm deep round cake tin with baking parchment, allowing the paper to come 2 cm above the rim.

Beat {{unsalted-butter}} of softened butter and {{dark-brown-sugar}} of dark brown sugar together until pale and fluffy, about 4 minutes. Add {{eggs}} eggs one at a time, beating well after each. If the mixture curdles, add a tablespoon of flour.

Fold in {{plain-flour}} of plain flour, {{baking-powder}} of baking powder, and {{almond-flour}} of ground almonds. Add {{mixed-dried-fruit}} of mixed fruit, {{mixed-peel}} of candied peel, {{glace-cherries}} of glacé cherries, and the orange zest. Stir in the whisky or brandy if using.
Spoon the batter into the prepared tin and smooth the top. Arrange {{almonds-whole}} of whole blanched almonds on the surface in concentric rings, pressing them gently into the batter.
Bake for 1 hour 30 minutes to 1 hour 45 minutes, until a skewer inserted in the centre comes out clean. Check after 1 hour: if the almonds are browning too fast, cover loosely with foil.
Cool completely in the tin before turning out. Wrap in baking parchment and store in a tin for at least two days before cutting.

items.cause: Batter too thin, or fruit too wet
items.fix: Coat the fruit in a tablespoon of flour before folding in. Make sure the butter and sugar are properly creamed so the batter holds the fruit.

items.symptom: Cake is raw in the centre after the stated time
items.cause: Oven too hot causing outside to set early, or tin not deep enough
items.fix: Use a deep tin and cover with foil. Lower temperature by 10°C and check again in 15 minutes.

items.cause: Not pressed in firmly enough before baking
items.fix: Press each almond into the batter so at least half is embedded. They set firm as the batter bakes.

content.text: Dundee cake is Scottish baking at its most restrained: rich but not heavy, fruit-packed but not dark. Unlike Christmas cake, it needs no feeding with alcohol over weeks, no marzipan, no royal icing. It is ready to eat in a few days and keeps for two weeks without difficulty. In Scotland it is eaten at teatime, at celebrations, and at Hogmanay. The whole almond top has come to represent the cake as much as any particular flavour: it is how you recognise a Dundee cake from across a table.
